clue.text: Marsupial reproductive organ initially astounded taxonomists

indicators.note: what is done initially is done at the very start, so only the opening letter of each word beside it is taken

blocks.note: the organ a mammal carries its unborn young in
the initial letters of the two words, in the order the clue prints them

explanation.walkthrough: A marsupial's young finish growing in the pouch rather than the womb, so the organ the wordplay borrows is the one this animal makes least use of.
explanation.definitionFit: Marsupial -> WOMBAT: definition by example, since the wombat is one particular Australian pouched animal and the clue names only the family.

clue.text: Burmese boarding houses served up super roly-poly

indicators.note: to house something is to keep it within your walls, so these words have the answer indoors
a dish comes up from the kitchen, and in a down entry coming up means reading from the bottom square towards the top

blocks.note: the tail of the first word and the head of the second give five letters in a row, and they read the right way only from the far end

explanation.walkthrough: A roly-poly is a suet pudding as well as a shape, which is what lets a boarding-house dinner and a description of a diner share one sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: super roly-poly -> OBESE: roly-poly is the nursery word for comfortably round, and pushing it to 'super' reaches the clinical term for dangerously overweight.

clue.text: Stupid Scandinavian spawned Spoonerism

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner traded the opening sounds of two words, so naming the trick is an instruction to swap them over

blocks.note: a Dane is a Scandinavian, and Spooner takes his D away and hands him a BR instead
spawned means bred, and it collects the D the Dane gave up

explanation.walkthrough: Say the setter's two words in his order first and swap afterwards; the hyphen in the enumeration is the promise that what comes out is one compound word.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupid -> BRAIN-DEAD: the medical term for irreversible loss of brain function, borrowed by everyday speech as an insult for someone showing no sign of thought.

clue.text: Hunter S dismissed as gossip?

indicators.note: a servant who is dismissed is sent away and does not come back, and the letter beside it goes the same way

blocks.note: the hunter is a STALKER, one who follows game unseen, and sacking the S it starts with leaves the six letters after it

explanation.walkthrough: Hunter S. Thompson is the whole misdirection: the middle initial belongs to the wordplay rather than to the journalist, and it is the letter being sacked.
explanation.definitionFit: gossip -> TALKER: a gossip is named for the single thing they do, and the plain agent noun for someone who does a lot of it says the same.

clue.text: Troublemakers playing REM single endlessly

indicators.note: a band plays a song, but letters played with are letters handled loosely enough to end up somewhere else
something endless never reaches its end, so the final letter of the word beside it is never written down

blocks.note: the band's three letters join the pile exactly as printed
a single stopped before its last letter supplies five more

explanation.walkthrough: Gremlins are the imaginary imps RAF crews blamed for machinery failing in the 1940s, and the name has outlived the aircraft it was invented for.
explanation.definitionFit: Troublemakers -> GREMLINS: a gremlin is the mischief-maker held responsible when a machine misbehaves, so the word names a whole class of small deliberate trouble.

clue.text: Enraged MAGA chants meet defending Democrat's victory statement

indicators.note: rage is the loss of all self-control, and letters that have lost control of themselves will not stay in the order given
a defender stands all round the thing being protected, so the rearranged letters close over the piece named next

blocks.note: fourteen letters dealt out again, and they part after nine to take something in
on a US ballot a Democrat's name carries a (D) after it

explanation.walkthrough: A rally between MAGA chanters and a Democrat is the picture; the answer is called from the umpire's chair instead, which is where a clue about a contest least wants you to look.
explanation.definitionFit: victory statement -> GAME SET AND MATCH: the umpire's words as a tennis match ends, used far beyond the court to announce a contest is settled.

clue.text: Cries of former international comprehended by reticent people

indicators.note: in its older sense to comprehend is to take something in and hold it, so the piece beside it swallows the other

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner, and EX- is the standing prefix for anything former
someone who clams up refuses to say anything, so a clam is a reticent person
an international is a player capped for their country, and I is the abbreviation for it; it lands between the A and the M

explanation.walkthrough: Reticent people who make cries of any kind are a contradiction, and the clue survives it because the two halves never meet: one is the definition, the other the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Cries -> EXCLAIMS: to exclaim is to cry out suddenly, so the definition is the everyday verb for the same short burst of speech.

clue.text: Odd characters fleeing flood in Rye Valley

indicators.note: number the letters along and let the first, third and fifth run away; every second one is left standing

blocks.note: ten letters, of which the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth stay behind

explanation.walkthrough: Rye is a Sussex town where flooding is a real worry, so the surface reads as local news while the letters are quietly being counted off in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Valley -> LOIRE: the Loire Valley is the chateau-lined stretch of central France, known to everyone by the river's name alone.

clue.text: Drunken bum slunk around Lima? Idiot!

indicators.note: a drunk cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state keep to no line either
to go around a thing is to pass on every side of it, so the rearranged letters close over the one named next

blocks.note: eight letters dealt out again, and they part before the last of them
Lima is how a radio operator says the letter L

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark after the city is doing real work: it warns that Peru is not wanted at all, only the letter the word stands for on the airwaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiot -> NUMBSKULL: literally a skull gone numb, so the word calls someone stupid by picturing a head that cannot feel anything.

clue.text: Lament extremely bizarre rule about nursing institute

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two far ends, so this one contributes only its outermost letters
something turned about is facing the other way, and these three letters are written in the opposite order
a nurse keeps a patient in her care, so the piece beside it is being held inside

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word, its two extremes
a rule laid down for everyone is a law, and here it is written backwards
I is the abbreviation for institute, as in a body's initials; it drops in between the A and the L

explanation.walkthrough: Four small operations in six words, and the sentence still reads as a grumble about red tape — that smoothness is the disguise, and 'nursing' is what gives it away.
explanation.definitionFit: Lament -> BEWAIL: to bewail a thing is to weep and cry out over it, an old-fashioned verb that survives mainly in writing and in crosswords.

clue.text: Chairman maintains church is centre of harmful masculinity

indicators.note: to maintain something is to keep hold of it, so this word keeps the others inside itself
the centre of a word is the letter with the same number standing either side of it

blocks.note: Chairman Mao ruled China from 1949, and the title alone is enough to name him
CH is what an Ordnance Survey map prints for a church
the verb is taken at face value, two letters as written
the middle letter of the seven, with three on each side

explanation.walkthrough: 'Harmful masculinity' is the phrase the surface wants read whole, and prising it apart is the solve: only the second word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: masculinity -> MACHISMO: the Spanish word for aggressive male pride, taken into English for masculinity of the strutting, something-to-prove kind.

clue.text: Turns nasty colour, repulsed by sulphur

indicators.note: an attack that is repulsed is driven straight back the way it came, and so are these three letters

blocks.note: a mean trick is a nasty one
the plainest colour of them all, and it arrives back to front
S is sulphur's symbol in the periodic table

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns nasty' is a phrase, and separating the two words is the whole clue: one of them is the definition and the other is four letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Turns -> MEANDERS: a river that meanders turns this way and that across flat ground, so the verb names continual wandering rather than one bend.

clue.text: Opposed state surveillance on vacation

indicators.note: a house whose owners are on vacation is empty in the middle, with only its outside left standing

blocks.note: to aver something is to state it firmly, a word that survives mostly in court
everything between its first letter and its last has gone away, leaving the two ends

explanation.walkthrough: 'State surveillance' is one idea on the surface and two separate jobs underneath, which is why a clue about spying reads so much like a headline.
explanation.definitionFit: Opposed -> AVERSE: to be averse to a thing is to be set against it, and the word almost always arrives with 'to' in front of what is opposed.

clue.text: District of Cadiz on escarpment

indicators.note: a district of a place is a piece taken from inside it, and this piece is taken from inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the four letters run across the joins, from the end of the Spanish port into the start of the slope

explanation.walkthrough: Cadiz and an escarpment make a plausible piece of geography, and geography is the one thing they are not doing here: they are only lending letters.
explanation.definitionFit: District -> ZONE: a zone is an area marked off and treated as a single unit, so it is the planner's word for what everyday speech calls a district.

clue.text: Deference award one kept in study overlooking empty countryside

indicators.note: a pupil kept in stays inside the building after everyone else has gone, and this letter stays inside the word
a house overlooking a field stands above it, and in a down entry standing above means coming first
an empty room has nothing between its walls, so only the first and last letters of the word remain

blocks.note: the Order of the British Empire, handed out at the palace twice a year
the Roman numeral for one
a den is the small room at home where the work gets done, and the I goes in after its D
its first and last letters, with everything between them cleared out

explanation.walkthrough: An award, a study and the countryside are the furniture of a settled English life, which is what stops the surface sounding like the list of instructions it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Deference -> OBEDIENCE: both name yielding to another's will, obedience being the doing of what you are told where deference is the respect behind it.

clue.text: Fearful rodent discovered on Southeast Asian island

indicators.note: read it as dis-covered: the covering comes off, and a word's covering is the letter at each end
in an across entry one thing sits on another by following it, so this piece goes at the back

blocks.note: the island at the far end of the Indonesian chain, shared with East Timor
the rodent is a MOUSE, and stripping a letter off each end leaves the middle three

explanation.walkthrough: Burns addressed a mouse as a 'wee, sleekit, cow'rin, tim'rous beastie', so the rodent and the definition have been sharing a line of verse since 1785.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearful -> TIMOROUS: timorous is built on timor, Latin for fear, and describes the one shrinking from a fright rather than the fright itself.

clue.text: Drag one's feet following concerning shake-up

indicators.note: what follows a thing comes after it, and in a down entry after means further down the column

blocks.note: RE heads a memo to mean concerning, from the Latin for 'in the matter of'
to shuffle is to walk without lifting your feet clear of the floor

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shake-up' sits at the end of the clue looking like an instruction to rearrange letters. It is the definition, and nothing in this one gets rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: shake-up -> RESHUFFLE: a cabinet reshuffle moves the same people into different jobs, which is exactly what a shake-up of an organisation amounts to.

clue.text: Pinch child squashing tiny insect

indicators.note: to squash a thing is to press down until it is flat under whatever is on top, so the piece named next ends up buried

blocks.note: a son is somebody's child, and the word opens up after its first letter
the biting fly of Scottish summers, small enough to fit inside

explanation.walkthrough: A child squashing an insect is a complete small scene, and it does the opposite of what it says: the insect ends up inside the child, entirely intact.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinch -> SMIDGEON: a pinch of salt is as much as finger and thumb will hold, and a smidgeon is the same vague, very small helping.

clue.text: Detective entertained by Melville's name for bucolic character

indicators.note: a host entertains a guest inside the house, so the letters beside it take the other piece in

blocks.note: the author of Moby-Dick was Herman Melville, and his first name parts after three letters
DS is a detective sergeant's rank as the police abbreviate it

explanation.walkthrough: Whale-hunting is nobody's idea of a pastoral scene, which makes Melville's own name a good place to keep a man who looks after cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: bucolic character -> HERDSMAN: bucolic means of the countryside and its herding life, so the figure the word conjures is the one driving the cattle.

clue.text: Piece one played very softly in auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is a room for hearing, so whatever happens there reaches you through the ear rather than the eye

blocks.note: to play very softly is to play so low, and the two words run together into one when you say them

explanation.walkthrough: Music sits on both sides of this clue, a dynamic marking on one and a performance on the other, so the ear is the only thing keeping them apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Piece one played -> SOLO: a solo is written for a single performer, so the definition names it by counting the people on stage.

clue.text: Seek over-the-counter drug when lacking in energy

indicators.note: to lack a thing is to be without it, so whatever is named next is missing from the word

blocks.note: ASPIRIN is the painkiller sold without a prescription, and it turns up here without its IN
E is the physicist's symbol for energy, as in E=mc2

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking in energy' reads as one weary phrase and has to be heard as two separate instructions, which is the whole of the disguise here.
explanation.definitionFit: Seek -> ASPIRE: to aspire to something is to seek it as an ambition, the sense of seeking that is about wanting rather than searching.

clue.text: Funny bone with a large diameter

blocks.note: one of the twelve pairs curving round the chest
the article is taken exactly as printed
L is the size printed on a clothing label
d stands for diameter in a geometry formula

explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny bone' is the phrase the surface offers and its two words belong to opposite halves of the clue, which is as neat a join as this grid has.
explanation.definitionFit: Funny -> RIBALD: ribald humour is the coarse, rude sort, so the definition offers the mildest available word for a joke that is anything but.

clue.text: An epoch reflected in entertainment venue

indicators.note: a reflection shows a thing the wrong way round, and these five letters are read back out of the mirror

blocks.note: the article is taken exactly as printed, two letters
an era is a stretch of history, the epoch of a geologist or a historian

explanation.walkthrough: Five letters that read as an ordinary scrap of English forwards and a concert venue backwards; the surface is doing nothing but supplying them.
explanation.definitionFit: entertainment venue -> ARENA: the Roman arena was the sanded floor where the spectacle took place, and the word now covers the whole building a tour plays in.

clue.text: Times desperately stifling question over inaccurate citation

indicators.note: a desperate person will try anything in any order, and letters handled that way come out in one
to stifle someone is to smother them by closing over their face, so these letters close over the ones named next

blocks.note: the paper's five letters dealt out again, then opened after three
qu. is the short form of question on a dictionary page or an exam paper
O is an over on a cricket scorecard

explanation.walkthrough: The italics mark the newspaper rather than the plural of time, so the surface is a paper getting a quotation wrong — and lending five of the eight letters to do it.
explanation.definitionFit: inaccurate citation -> MISQUOTE: to misquote is to report someone's words wrongly, with MIS- doing its usual job of turning an action into a botched one.

clue.text: Seduce office worker close to retirement

indicators.note: the close of anything is its end, so only the final letter of the word beside it is wanted

blocks.note: a temp is the agency worker brought in to cover a desk for a week
the letter the word closes on

explanation.walkthrough: An office worker close to retirement is a whole person in five words, and the clue needs you to stop seeing them and start counting letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Seduce -> TEMPT: both mean drawing someone towards what they should resist, tempt being the older and milder of the two, as in tempting fate.

clue.text: Entire broadcast about New Hampshire native

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it by hand, so what is broadcast lands in no particular order
one thing set about another is wrapped round it, so these letters open to let the next piece in

blocks.note: the six letters dealt out again, and they part after the first
NH is the state's two-letter postal code

explanation.walkthrough: 'Native' is the definition hiding in plain sight, because a native of New Hampshire is the obvious reading and the state is only there for two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: native -> INHERENT: an inherent quality is one born in the thing itself, which is the older sense of native, belonging by birth rather than by nationality.

clue.text: Popular fellow beginning to appreciate setter's notoriety

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is the letter it starts with, and that is all this one contributes

blocks.note: whatever is in this season is what is popular
F is the abbreviation for fellow, as after the name of a Royal Society member
the first letter of the word
the setter is the voice writing the clue, so anything of the setter's is mine

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter's' means 'my' wherever a crossword says it — the setter speaks the clue in the first person — and it is one of the earliest conventions worth owning.
explanation.definitionFit: notoriety -> INFAMY: infamy is fame gone bad, so the definition is the neutral-sounding noun for being widely known for the wrong reasons.

clue.text: A filling meal after essentially free promotional event

indicators.note: a filling goes into the hole in a tooth, so this letter drops into the word rather than sitting beside it
the essence of a word is what sits at its heart once the outsides are taken away
what comes after a thing is written behind it, so the piece named first takes the front

blocks.note: the two letters at the heart of the word, with the F and the last E taken off
the midday meal, and it opens up after its first letter
the article is taken exactly as printed, and it is what goes into the gap

explanation.walkthrough: 'A filling meal' is one idea on the surface and three instructions underneath, which is how a clue about lunch turns out to be about marketing.
explanation.definitionFit: promotional event -> RELAUNCH: a product sent back to market with new packaging, and the party thrown to announce it takes the same name.

clue.text: Releases tip of willie caught in flies!

indicators.note: the tip of a thing is its far end, so what is wanted is the letter the word finishes on
whatever is caught in something is held inside it, so this letter sits among the others rather than beside them

blocks.note: the letter at the very end of the word
jets are aircraft, so 'flies' is a noun here and not a verb
c is how a cricket scorecard records a batsman caught, and it drops in after the second letter

explanation.walkthrough: The seaside-postcard surface is the joke, and every word of it turns out respectable: a trouser zip, some aircraft and a line of a cricket score.
explanation.definitionFit: Releases -> EJECTS: a machine ejects a cassette by pushing it out, so the definition is the gentler word for the same forcible letting-go.
